x: From nothing to a running console and your first detections. Build aertun, create a store and its first administrator, sign in with a passkey, then connect a source, install detections and decide who else may do what. Build it#Go 1.27 or later is the only requirement. There is nothing else to fetch.git clone https://github.com/aertun/aertun aertun && cd aertun go build -o aertun ./cmd/aertun Create a store and its Owner#./aertun init --owner you@example.comIt makes you the store's Owner and prints a one-time link that adds your passkey. There is no default password and no default account. Everybody else you add is a collaborator with a role; see Roles. Start the console and add your passkey#./aertun serveThe console listens on 127.0.0.1:8080. Open the link init printed, add a passkey, and you are signed in. Follow Get started#Get started in the console walks four things: bring events in, decide what counts as wrong, know the estate, and decide who else may do what. It reads the store rather than telling a story, so each step is ticked when it is done.

Once anybody is an administrator, a command run from a terminal needs a token, which proves who is running it. Issuing an administrator's token takes a second administrator, so ask for yours, approve it in the console, where Approvals lists it, and collect it within a day: aertun token issue you --principal you@example.com --role admin aertun pending redeem ID The token is printed once. Keep it in ~/.aertun/token, or pass it as AERTUN_TOKEN or --token. The same first steps, from the terminal: aertun vault enable aertun connect add okta --org example AERTUN_CONNECT_SECRET=... aertun connect secret okta aertun collect run aertun detect pack install aertun detect run aertun estate build aertun auth enrol sam@example.com aertun auth grant sam@example.com analyst See Connectors and feeds, Detections, Estate and workforce and People for each.
The first screen after signing in is Today: what is waiting for you to decide, then what is wrong in the parts of the estate you work in.
The box in the bar finds a screen or a setting by the words you would use for it. There is no query syntax: every word is looked up, and a colon, a quote or a bracket is part of a word.

Get the program, and run it the way it is meant to be run. Build aertun from source with Go alone, install it with make, run it under systemd or in a distroless container, and put it behind a reverse proxy.

Go 1.27 or later, and nothing else: go.mod has no require block, so the standard library and the Go toolchain are the whole build. make sudo make install make install honours prefix and DESTDIR, and sudo make uninstall removes it. Without make: go build -o aertun ./cmd/aertun install -m 0755 aertun /usr/local/bin/

docker build -t aertun . docker run --rm -v aertun:/srv aertun --root /srv/store init --owner you@example.com docker run -p 8080:8080 -v aertun:/srv aertun The first command prints the link that adds your passkey; open it once the second is running. The image is the binary alone on gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot: no shell, no package manager, no interpreter and no libc. It runs as nonroot and carries LICENSE and NOTICE.

There is no tagged release yet. When there is, the release workflow publishes a static binary for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, with SHA256SUMS, a build provenance attestation for each, and the image ghcr.io/aertun/aertun. Check a binary before you run it: sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS gh attestation verify aertun-linux-amd64 --repo aertun/aertun

Set admin.base_url to the address people use and admin.behind_tls_proxy to true. The repository's deploy/ folder has a systemd unit and a Caddy configuration. aertun config set admin.base_url https://aertun.example.com aertun config set admin.behind_tls_proxy true

The terms this manual uses, defined once. Short definitions of the words the aertun manual and console use: sources, events, detections, findings, cases, regimes, playbooks, actions, the audit log. SourceWhere events come from: a connector reading another tool's API, a log file mapped by a source mapping, or a feed another system pushes to. EventOne thing that happened, mapped to one shape and kept append-only in the event store before anything reads it. Detection ruleA declared condition over events, with fixtures it must match and must not. A rule is live, in the trial ring (it records what it would raise) or off. FindingSomething a rule, a correlation or an automation says is wrong. Its state is open, triaged, accepted, fixed, stale, false-positive or benign, and every decision on it is kept. Case, incidentA record of something being handled, graded sev1 to sev4, with the notification duties of each regime that applies. RegimeA law with a notification clock: GDPR (eu), NIS2, DORA, the Cyber Resilience Act (cra), SEC, CIRCIA or HIPAA. A clock starts when somebody records the decision it runs from, or when an earlier report it is timed from is recorded as done. PlaybookSteps for a kind of incident, proposed, approved and then worked through step by step. ActionOne declared thing done to another platform, such as suspending an Okta account. Asked for by one person, approved by another. AutomationA rule of the form when this happens, if this is true, do this, in one of three modes: watch, ask or act. EstateThe people who work here and what they use, joined across the tools that know about them. SSVC, VEXSSVC is the decision tree that turns a vulnerability's facts into what to do; VEX is the published statement of whether a product is affected. Audit logThe append-only record of every change aertun makes, hash-chained, signed and anchored.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: A claim about security work, checked by a program against evidence its author did not write, and signed whatever the verdict. Check detection rules, the AI analyst's threshold and other vendors' AI verdicts against evidence they did not write, and sign the verdict. A model can draft a detection rule faster than anybody can check it. A proof is the check, made by a program rather than by the author, and written down so whoever receives the rule — a reviewer, CI, a customer — can rely on it without trusting whoever handed it over.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: VerdictMeans provenevery check passed on evidence that could have failed it refuteda check failed, and the proof names what inconclusivenothing failed, but nothing could have: a rule checked only against its own fixtures A refutation is signed like a proof: what did not work is what the next attempt most needs to know.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun content keygen --out root.key # once: a signing key in the store; move root.key off the machine aertun proof detection --rule rule.json --corpus corpus.jsonl \ --key .aertun/content/release.key --public-key proof-key.json \ --out rule.proof.json --by you@example.com It checks, in order: valid — the rule is a rule; an invalid one is refuted and nothing else runs. fixtures — its own must-match and must-not-match examples hold. Necessary, never enough. corpus — over a labelled corpus (one JSON object a line, as aertun detect replay reads), it fires on every entry labelled as its own and on nothing else it reads. A false positive somebody recorded and nobody fixed still refutes it. Recall and specificity are reported as 95% Wilson lower bounds, so a proof over one example reads as the weak thing it is. Without a corpus the best verdict is inconclusive. --model and --prompt-sha256 record which model wrote the rule and a digest of its prompt — never the prompt.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun proof verify --key proof-key.json --subject rule.json rule.proof.json Both signatures must hold against a key you were handed, never one the document supplies; --subject checks the proof is about exactly that file. It exits non-zero on anything but proven, so it is a CI gate.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun analyst calibrate --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out calibration.json \ --epsilon 0.05 --delta 0.05 aertun analyst triage --calibration calibration.json --calibration-key proof-key.json The findings verified people have ruled are put to the configured model, and the lowest threshold is fitted at which closing suggestions on findings people ruled real stay under --epsilon with confidence one minus --delta — an exact Clopper–Pearson bound, corrected for every threshold examined. The certificate names the model, the adapter and the prompt template by digest, and expires. Triage gates on it only when it verifies and fits; one that does not, and any answer not scored on the channel it was fitted on, goes to a person rather than back to the declared threshold.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun verdict import charlotte.csv --source charlotte aertun verdict prove --source charlotte --since 2026-10-01 --tolerance 0.01 \ --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out charlotte.proof.json The export carries the columns alert, verdict and at, and optionally confidence, disposition, disposition_at and source; a file with any other column, such as the product's reasoning, is refused whole. Each verdict is joined to the decision a verified person made on the finding that alert raised here — the source's mapping names the path its alert id is at as alert — and only verdicts given before the decision count. The claim is about false closures, alerts the product closed that a person found real, against a tolerance you declare first: refuted when the exact lower bound is over it, naming the alerts; proven when the upper bound is at or under it on at least 30 closures; inconclusive between. The rate is over the closures somebody decided, which are not a random sample, so the proof states that coverage, and how many verdicts were delivered here before the decision rather than resting on the product's own clock.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun adjudicate size --rate 0.01 # how many closures a target needs: 299 aertun adjudicate draw --source charlotte --since 2026-10-01 --per 299 aertun adjudicate next SAMPLE # or the console's Adjudication screen aertun adjudicate judge SAMPLE --item 4 --judgement real --because "…" aertun adjudicate prove SAMPLE --tolerance 0.01 --key signing.key --out adjudication.proof.json A verdicts proof counts the closures somebody happened to decide, and people look again at what looked wrong. Here a sample is drawn at random from every closure the product's AI made in the period, reviewed or not, and from every closure people made, and its seed and digests are committed to the signed audit log before any item is shown; anybody holding the seed and the population can recompute the selection. Each item is shown with its evidence and nothing that says who closed it, how, or which of the two it came from. Nobody who closed an item may judge it, each is judged once, agents may not see the queue, and a judgement is a record in the log, never a decision on the finding — a product that learns from analysts cannot learn the answers. The proof reads the AI's share judged real against the tolerance, as a verdicts proof does, and reports the people's share beside it. It is refused unless every item of the committed sample was judged after the commitment by a verified person, and it says how many samples of the same product were drawn before it.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: aertun claim register charlotte-98 --source charlotte --metric agreement \ --direction at-least --threshold 0.98 --window-days 30 aertun claim list # or the console's Claim cards screen aertun claim test charlotte-98 --key signing.key --out charlotte-98.proof.json "98% agreement" can be made true afterwards by choosing the metric, the alerts, the period and the day to stop looking. A card fixes all of them first — the metric (agreement, false-closures, escalations-closed, abstentions, consistency or adjudicated-false-closures), the product, the labels and severity floor, the threshold and its direction, the confidence and the window — and commits its digest to the signed audit log. Only data that arrives after that entry counts; a card is never changed, and one edited on disk matches no registration and is refused. claim test signs what it finds and decides nothing while the window is open: a test run every day and kept the day it passed is not pre-registered. Once it has closed, the exact interval at the card's own confidence proves the claim when the bound on the claimed side clears the threshold, on at least 30 alerts, and refutes it when the bound on the other side fails it. A card for adjudicated-false-closures is tested on the one blind sample drawn for it after it was registered, with aertun adjudicate draw --claim NAME.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Hold an agent to its own account
x: aertun agent maps triage-bot --host build01 # once: where it runs aertun agent reconcile triage-bot --since 2026-11-01 --telemetry triage-bot \ --key signing.key --public-key proof-key.json --out triage-bot.proof.json The agent's account is the tool calls its GenAI telemetry reported, under the identity --telemetry declares (its gen_ai.agent.id; the registered name by default). It is held against what Aertun saw without asking it: every call the agent interface answered for the agent, from the signed audit log once the log verifies, and every connection the recorder saw leave a machine declared to run that agent and no other. A call is matched to the agent's report of the same tool within --window (two minutes by default), however its host prefixed the tool's name. refuted names what is unaccounted for: a call it did not report, a call it reports and the server never received, a connection while it reported nothing. An agent that reported nothing while it was seen acting is refuted, and the proof says it cannot tell that from one never instrumented. proven needs at least ten observations with nothing unaccounted for; inconclusive is fewer. A machine declared for several agents, or under a name a proof cannot carry, is counted and left out; what the agent did in other systems is not covered, because nothing ties it to its identity there.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
s: Kept proofs, and the Proofs screen
x: aertun proof keep rule.proof.json --public-key proof-key.json aertun proof list [--kind detection|calibration|verdicts|reconciliation|adjudication|claim] aertun proof show ID verdict prove, analyst calibrate, agent reconcile, adjudicate prove and claim test (once its window has closed) keep the proofs they make; a proof made elsewhere — in CI, on another deployment — is kept with proof keep, or from the Proofs screen under Proving ground, only after it verifies against the key handed in with it. The key is kept beside it by fingerprint: verifying says the key signed it, and whether that key is one to believe is yours to judge. A kept proof is checked again every time it is read, so one edited afterwards is listed as no longer verifying rather than as what it now says. Listing and reading are what the agent interface offers, as list_proofs and read_proof, every value labelled with whether somebody outside Aertun could have written it. A detection proof's rule name is the submitter's, perhaps the model under test, so the screen marks it untrusted where the agent interface labels it. Keeping a proof is a change, and no agent may make one.

p: Proofs: AI work checked and signed
x: An in-toto Statement in a DSSE envelope: the subject is the rule file by digest; the predicate (https://aertun.github.io/proof/detection/v1) names the claim in words, the verifier and its version, every material it read by digest, each check, and the verdict. It is signed twice, Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65, the second in the context aertun/proof/v1. The Ed25519 half is plain DSSE, so in-toto and Sigstore tooling check it with no help from Aertun. The signing key file must be readable by its owner alone.

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: Scripted attacks on AI agents, replayed through your detections, scored and signed. Replay scripted malicious AI-agent sessions through a recorded stream, measure whether the detections caught them, and sign a scorecard anybody can verify. The wind tunnel splices scripted malicious agent sessions into a recorded telemetry stream in a scratch store and measures whether the detections caught them. Nothing live is touched: the exfiltration step is a log line about exfiltration, written to a scratch spool. aertun windtunnel list-scenarios aertun windtunnel preflight aertun windtunnel run --key .aertun/content/release.key --public-key scorecard-key.json --out scorecard.json aertun windtunnel verify --key scorecard-key.json scorecard.json aertun windtunnel diff old.json new.json # the CI gate: fails on a regression

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: A scenario is data, never code: a malicious agent session as the security operations centre would see it, with a benign twin doing the legitimate version of the same work, on which nothing may fire. Six ship today: an injection through an issue, an MCP server's rug-pull, a read-then-exfiltrate chain, a slopsquatted install, a runaway cost loop, and a blind window in the recorder.

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: It names what ran before how it went — scenario digests, the stream's digest, the rule pack's version — then reports the miss rate first, with 95% Wilson bounds, and per family. Sealed with its own digest and signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65, so a third party verifies it offline with the public key alone.

p: The wind tunnel: attacks on AI agents, replayed
x: By default the scorecard is scored against Aertun's own reference rules, which were written beside the scenarios: it is a regression test of that pack, not an independent measurement. run --sigma DIR scores your own Sigma rules instead, joined at ATT&CK technique level, with the join's limits stated on the document.

Everything waiting for you to decide, in one place. One screen for everything waiting for you: actions on other platforms, runs an automation held, and privileged changes that need a second administrator. Three things wait for a person, and each is decided by somebody other than whoever asked for it: An action on another platform, asked for on a case. A run an automation held, because its mode is ask. A privileged change: making somebody an administrator, issuing an administrator's token, weakening a setting, lowering how many approvals a change needs, or moving the audit log. aertun approvals aertun incident act-approve ID N aertun automate approve RUN aertun pending approve ID What was asked for, by whom and why is shown before anybody decides, and the decision is in the audit log.

s: When you are the only administrator
x: A privileged change asked for by the only administrator is slowed, not blocked: It needs a reason, given with the command's own option (--note on a grant, --why on an administrator's token or an audit log move, --accept-risk on a weaker setting) or written on the screen. The reason is kept in the request and in its audit record, because nobody else's approval stands beside it. It waits an hour — a day to move the audit log or pass on ownership — and Aertun's detections over its own audit log raise it. Any administrator's session can decline it while it waits. Approving your own request needs a passkey sign-in from the last five minutes. The People screen asks for your passkey when your sign-in is older; a command-line token is not a passkey sign-in, so aertun pending approve points you to the screen for your own requests. The record says the change was approved alone.

One queue, ranked by risk, and every decision kept. One queue of security findings ranked by risk, decisions kept and replayable, and an AI analyst that suggests a verdict from counts without ever recording one. Read the queue#aertun finding list --state open aertun finding risk aertun finding story ID Let the analyst take the first pass#aertun analyst plan aertun analyst triage --limit 20 --dry-runThe model is any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set with AERTUN_MODEL_URL, AERTUN_MODEL_KEY and AERTUN_MODEL. Without one, findings are triaged by people alone. Decide#aertun finding decide ID false-positiveThe states are open, triaged, accepted, fixed, stale, false-positive and benign.

s: What a log line cannot do to the analyst
x: A finding's evidence is log text, written by whoever reached the log. So nothing depends on the model declining an instruction, and the worst a planted line can do is make a suggestion wrong: What it reads, and in what order, is a plan fixed in code. Nothing a log says can add a step. It is given counts and closed words the program worked out, and, separately and marked, the text somebody else wrote. Its answer is one word from a closed set with a confidence, shown only above a threshold. The reason a person reads is assembled from the counts, never from what the model wrote. Personal data and credentials are masked before the prompt leaves and restored in the answer. A person records the verdict; the analyst has no way to. aertun analyst eval --k 3 measures it against what people decided.
aertun detect replay runs today's rules over the events again and says which decisions would now be different, and aertun detect learn FINDING turns a decision into a fixture.

Incidents with the clocks each law starts, and actions a second person approves. Incidents with the clocks GDPR, NIS2, DORA, the Cyber Resilience Act, SEC, CIRCIA and HIPAA start, playbooks, and actions a second person approves. Choose the regimes that apply#aertun incident regimes eu nis2With none set, a new incident starts with no obligations and no clocks. Declare an incident#aertun incident declare --title "Token used from an unknown country" --grade sev2 --finding ID Start the clocks#A clock starts when somebody decides the organisation is aware, and that decision is recorded with its reason.aertun incident decide ID aware --because "..." aertun incident duties Discharge or waive each duty#aertun incident discharge ID "NIS2 early warning" --because "sent to the CSIRT" aertun incident waive ID "GDPR Article 34" --because "no personal data involved" Work a playbook#aertun incident playbooks aertun incident propose ID account-compromise aertun incident step ID account-compromise STEP done --because "..."The shipped playbooks cover account compromise, phishing, malware on an endpoint, a lost device and exposed data. Act on another platform, with a second person#aertun action add okta-suspend-user --org example aertun incident act ID okta-suspend-user okta:USER --because "..." aertun incident act-approve ID 1The exact request is shown before anybody approves it, and it is sent only when a second person does. Some reports are timed from an earlier one rather than from a decision — NIS2's final report a month after its notification, DORA's intermediate report 72 hours after the initial notification and its final report a month after that — so their clocks start when the earlier report is recorded as done. Months are counted as EU law counts them: a month from 31 January ends on the last day of February. DORA's initial notification is due four hours after classification as major and no later than 24 hours after awareness. The Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties (regime cra) apply to manufacturers from 11 September 2026; its final report on an exploited vulnerability runs from aertun incident decide ID mitigated. CIRCIA's 72 hours are shown with a note that reporting is required only once CISA's final rule takes effect. The deadlines are the published ones, counted from the decision, not legal advice. Notices to the people affected are drafted, planned and sent with aertun notify.

What happened, kept append-only, and what is rare enough to look at. Every event mapped to one shape and kept append-only, with retention and legal holds, identity links across platforms, and a hunt that shows what is rare.
aertun spool stats aertun spool verify aertun spool retain --apply aertun spool hold NAME --why "litigation hold" Retention never deletes what a hold covers, and a hold is lifted by name.
aertun identity link okta:00u1abc dana@example.com aertun identity list

aertun telemetry fields events.jsonl aertun hunt --field raw.user_agent --by actor events.jsonl aertun triage events.jsonl --rules ./rules A hunt counts one field's values and shows the rarest, which is what is worth a look. The Hunt screen does the same over the store, and offers what you found as the start of a rule.

Indicators of compromise, from STIX 2.1 bundles or plain lists. Import indicators of compromise from STIX 2.1 bundles or plain lists, add them one at a time, and see which events and findings they match. aertun intel import bundle.json --source "isac" aertun intel add 203.0.113.7 --source "case 12" aertun intel list aertun intel remove ID A STIX 2.1 bundle's indicators are read from their patterns. A pattern with AND, a time qualifier, a wildcard or a range is reported as not read, never guessed at. A plain list carries one value to a line, defanged or not. Each indicator keeps the source it came from, so a match says who said it was bad, and the events already held are searched for it when it arrives.

Rules with fixtures, Sigma import, a trial ring, and suppressions that end. Write detection rules with fixtures, import Sigma, trial a rule before it reaches the queue, correlate across platforms, and suppress noise with an end date. Install the shipped rules#aertun detect pack install aertun detect testEach rule carries fixtures it must match and must not, MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs, and a line on what it does not catch. Bring your own, in the open standard#aertun sigma import ./rules Trial a rule before it reaches the queue#aertun detect ring RULE trial --because "new rule" aertun detect stats aertun detect ring RULE live --because "a week without a false positive"In the trial ring a rule records what it would raise, and its record earns it the queue. Suppress, until a date#aertun detect suppress RULE user.name=svc-backup --owner dana --until 2026-12-31 --because "known job" Correlations raise a finding about several events across rules and platforms, once their window closes; aertun correlate demo shows one end to end.

When this happens, do this: rules that watch, ask, or act within limits. Automation rules of the form when this happens, do this, in watch, ask or act mode, with limits, approvals by a second person, and sign-in rules for step-up. aertun automate templates aertun automate add TEMPLATE aertun automate mode ID ask aertun automate runs aertun automate approve RUN Watch records what the rule would do. Ask waits for a person to approve each run. Act does it at once, within an hourly limit per rule, so one noisy source cannot suspend everybody. Whoever wrote a rule does not approve the runs it holds. Approving a run that acts on people's access takes an administrator of all of aertun. Rules about sign-ins can tell an office or a VPN from anywhere else: aertun geo network add 198.51.100.0/24 head-office --kind office aertun geo status

Read other tools through their APIs, map their logs, and take what they push. Read Okta, Entra ID, GitHub, KnowBe4, Vanta and more through their APIs, map logs from 17 platforms to one shape, and receive SSF, CAEP and webhook feeds.

A connector reads one tool through its API, over only the endpoints its manifest declares, with a credential sealed under aertun's keyring. With no keyring, no credential can be stored. aertun vault enable aertun connect catalogue aertun connect add okta --org example aertun connect check okta AERTUN_CONNECT_SECRET=... aertun connect secret okta aertun connect run okta --save A region is chosen from the connector's own list, never typed as a hostname, so adding a connector cannot point a credential at another machine. The catalogue says which credential each needs and the least it should be allowed to do. Shipped connectors: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, GitHub, EVM smart contracts through a Blockscout explorer, KnowBe4, ManageEngine Endpoint Central, ManageEngine MDM Plus and Vanta. aertun connect probe shows the shape of a response, never its values.

aertun collect run aertun collect file aws/cloudtrail trail.json aertun collect auto 15m Logs are mapped to one shape from AWS CloudTrail, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Azure, Google Workspace, Google Cloud, Okta, Duo, CrowdStrike Falcon, Jamf Pro, GitHub, Kubernetes, Cloudflare, Salesforce, Slack, Snowflake, Linux auditd and EVM chains. aertun source add adds a mapping of your own, checked against a sample, and aertun telemetry check says whether what it produces can be used at all.

aertun inbound add ssf corp-idp aertun inbound add okta okta-hooks aertun inbound add webhook ci aertun inbound status NAME A feed's endpoint is /feeds/NAME on the console. Shared Signals (SSF, CAEP, RISC) are verified against the transmitter's keys; webhooks against their secret. What arrives is stored like anything collected, and put to the automations as a signal.

Decide vulnerabilities, publish what you decided, and fix the ones that matter. Rank vulnerabilities with CISA KEV and EPSS, decide them with SSVC, publish OpenVEX, scan SBOMs against OSV, import SARIF, and plan upgrades clearing most risk. Import what is known#aertun vuln import --bom sbom.json --where api --osv osv.json --kev kev.json --epss epss.csv aertun vuln reach --source ./src --where apireach reads the asset's source for the symbols each open advisory names, and records what it found against that advisory. Say what each asset is#aertun vuln asset ISSUER:VALUE --exposure open --impact high --because "public API"Exposure is small, controlled or open; impact is low, medium, high or very high. Read the queue and the plan#aertun vuln queue aertun vuln plan aertun vuln why CVE-2026-0001The plan is the smallest set of upgrades that clears the most risk. Decide, and publish#aertun vuln assess CVE-2026-0001 PKG not_affected aertun vuln accept CVE-2026-0002 PKG --owner dana --until 2027-01-31 --because "..." aertun vuln vex --author "Example Ltd" --id https://example.com/vex/1The statuses are affected, fixed, not_affected and under_investigation. A risk acceptance names its owner, its end date and its reason.
aertun sca scan --bom sbom.json --osv db.json aertun sarif read results.sarif aertun appsec triage

Who works here, what they use, how exposed each is, and reminders that close the gaps. Join who works here with their devices, training and accounts across your tools, see where coverage is missing, send reminders, and review vendors and access. aertun estate build aertun estate scores --limit 20 aertun workforce coverage aertun workforce gaps aertun remind preview aertun remind send The estate joins the people your identity provider knows with the devices, training records and accounts other tools report, leavers included. A person's score is a file on an employee, so the Workforce risk screen is for administrators only, and the MCP interface shows only numbers, never names.

aertun vendor reconcile aertun vendor review ID aertun access open q4 identities.jsonl --scope okta,github --due 2026-12-10 aertun access decide q4 okta:00u1abc revoke aertun access close q4 identities-after.jsonl Each account is kept, revoked or reduced. A review closes on a later import, which shows whether what was decided was done; without one, a revocation is reported as unverified.

Who may do what, granted on a path, ending when it should. Grant roles and jobs on a path, deny what a broader grant would allow, explain any decision, provision people with SCIM, and issue tokens that end. aertun auth grant sam@example.com analyst aertun auth grant lee@example.com engineer --for 30d aertun auth deny sam@example.com responder --on /security/vulns aertun auth explain sam@example.com respond aertun auth list explain walks every binding and says which one decided, and why the others did not. See Roles for what each role may do.
aertun scim token aertun scim map security-analysts analyst aertun scim status The identity provider adds, changes and removes people; a group is mapped to a role or a job.

aertun token issue ci --principal ci-bot aertun token list aertun token revoke ID aertun token stale A token is shown once and stored only as a hash. An administrator's token takes a second administrator.

One Owner, collaborators with roles, and the duties kept apart. One Owner, then collaborators with a role (viewer, analyst, responder, admin) or a job, and duties kept apart so nobody, and no agent, acts alone.

A store starts with one person, its Owner: aertun init --owner NAME. The Owner holds the administrator role over the whole store, and nothing can take it away — not another administrator, not single sign-on provisioning, not a deny, not an end date. Ownership moves only when the Owner asks for a transfer and confirms it a day later; any administrator can decline it before then, and Aertun's own detections raise the request. aertun auth owner aertun auth owner transfer lee@example.com --note "handing over" # a day later, the Owner confirms it on the People screen with their passkey The new Owner must already administer the whole store with no end date.

Everybody else is a collaborator. aertun auth invite NAME ROLE grants the role and prints the one-time link that adds their passkey, in one step; the People screen does the same with "And give them a passkey enrolment link". Making somebody an administrator still waits for a second administrator, and the link is printed anyway, with the plain statement that signing in reaches nothing until the grant is approved. aertun auth grant and aertun auth enrol do the two halves separately. RoleMay viewerread findings, cases, the vulnerability queue and the dashboards analysttriage findings, open cases and add notes to them, hunt through events responderrun cases, ask for an action on another platform, approve somebody else's action, accept a risk adminmanage people, connectors and their credentials, and settings Each role includes the ones before it. Beside the ladder are jobs, for a different kind of work rather than more of it: an engineer tunes detections and automation rules, a vuln-manager decides vulnerabilities, and an auditor reads the queue and the audit log for a set time, after which the grant ends by itself. A grant can cover everything or only the security area (--on /@security), can end (--for 30d), and a deny always wins. There are deliberately no custom roles: assembling permissions is how a role surface stops being reviewable. aertun auth roles prints the whole model.

An action on another platform is approved by somebody other than whoever asked. Whoever wrote an automation rule does not approve the runs it holds. Making somebody an administrator, issuing an administrator's token, weakening a setting, lowering how many approvals a change needs and moving the audit log each take a second administrator. An only administrator is slowed, not blocked: their own request needs a reason, waits an hour (a day to move the audit log or pass on ownership), is raised by Aertun's detections over its own audit log, can be declined from any administrator's session, and only then may they approve it themselves, with a passkey sign-in from the last five minutes. The record says it was approved alone. Agents propose; people decide. An AI agent's authority is the intersection of its registry entry, the live grants of the person it acts for, and its token's own limits. It may ask for a privileged change, but never approve one, approve an action on another platform, or move ownership.

OpenID Connect and SAML, counted as two factors only when the provider says so. Sign in through OpenID Connect or SAML. Single sign-on counts as two factors only when the identity provider says it used them, or a passkey is asked for.
aertun oidc configure aertun oidc check aertun oidc status
aertun saml presets aertun saml add aertun saml metadata aertun saml list

A sign-in through the identity provider counts as two factors only when the provider says it used them: for OpenID Connect, the amr and acr claims with a recent auth_time; for SAML, the authentication context. When it does not say, aertun asks for the person's passkey as well.

Sign in with a passkey that checks it is you, and recover without a password. Sign in with a passkey that checks it is you, add one through a one-time enrolment link, lock out failed sign-ins by place, and recover without a password.
aertun auth enrol sam@example.com --for 24h It prints a one-time link that adds that person's passkey and does nothing else. Give it to them the way you would give a key; --revoke ends it.
Every passkey must check it is you, with a PIN, a fingerprint or a face, at registration and at every sign-in (NIST SP 800-63B-4). A security key with no PIN is asked to set one.

Failures lock out the places they come from, not the person: from where you usually sign in, or with your passkey, you still can. After many consecutive failures from anywhere, the method is disabled until the person proves themselves another way or an administrator lets it work again. aertun auth unlock sam@example.com

Every setting, what it does, and why a weaker value needs a second administrator. Every aertun setting with what it does and its default. A weaker value needs a recorded reason and a second administrator, and bounds no reason steps past. aertun config list aertun config explain session.idle aertun config set session.idle 30m aertun config unset session.idle Every default is the safer value. Setting a weaker one needs --accept-risk and a reason that is recorded, and then goes to a second administrator before it applies. Some settings have hard bounds no reason steps outside, such as the hour NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets for an unused session. SettingWhat it is session.idle, session.maxHow long a session lasts unused (an hour, at most), and at most in all. Anybody who can grant access is signed out after fifteen minutes unused. admin.base_url, admin.behind_tls_proxyThe console's public address, and whether a proxy in front of it ends TLS. network.modeOpen, or offline: refuse every connection that would leave the host. auth.throttle.*When failed sign-ins start to be delayed, and how long a delay grows. security.contactWhere your security team is reached. siem.stream.urlWhere the audit log is sent as it is written. passkey.require_hardware, passkey.authenticatorsWhich authenticators may hold a passkey. token.ttl.default, token.ttl.maxHow long a token lasts by default, and at most.

An append-only, signed, anchored record, and a stream of it to another SIEM. An append-only audit log: a hash chain, a Merkle tree, heads signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA, anchored to Bitcoin, written by its own process, streamed out. aertun auditlog verify aertun auditlog show SEQ aertun auditlog prove SEQ aertun auditlog head --save aertun auditlog consistency Every change is a record in a hash chain, with a Merkle tree over it. A tree head is signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA (post-quantum), and prove gives a receipt anybody can check against a head.

aertun auditlog anchor submit aertun auditlog anchor upgrade aertun auditlog anchor status The head is committed to Bitcoin through OpenTimestamps, so rewriting history is detectable by somebody who never trusted the operator.

aertun logd aertun logd status Run as its own account, the log writer is the only process that writes the log, so the console cannot rewrite what it recorded. A decision that is nothing but its record is reported as failed when the record cannot be written.

aertun config set siem.stream.url https://siem.example.com/ingest aertun siem stream key aertun siem stream status Batches of OCSF, each following the last exactly, each carrying a signed tree head and an HTTP message signature (RFC 9421), so the receiver can prove nothing was dropped or changed. aertun siem ocsf, cef and jsonl export the log as files.

Its own network purposes, sealed credentials, separate log writer and session limits. What aertun may connect to and why, credentials sealed in a vault, a separate log writer, two factors for all, session limits and an AI that only suggests.

aertun network Every outbound connection is for one declared purpose: an action, anchoring, a connector, mail, the AI analyst's model, the SIEM stream, shared signals, Slack reminders, single sign-on and notice webhooks. An undeclared purpose is refused in every mode, and network.mode offline refuses everything that would leave the host.

aertun vault status aertun vault rotate A connector's credentials and a feed's secret are sealed under a keyring, so the store's files alone give nobody the values: a lost laptop, a backup on an open bucket, a disposed disk. With no keyring, none can be stored.

Everybody signs in with two factors: a passkey that checks it is them, or single sign-on that says it used two. Failed sign-ins lock out places, not people, and sessions end after an hour unused, fifteen minutes for anybody who can grant access.
The AI analyst and agents over MCP read and propose. Neither can record a decision, approve an action, change who may do what, or reach another platform. See Findings and AI agents over MCP.

Eight operations behind three tools, for an agent that reads and proposes.
